fixes.explanation: Nice thought, baker, since a harvest is a happy word. But the text says the message concerned a great conflict (Daniel 10:1). It was also true, and Daniel got the understanding of it in a vision.

Not quite, baker. The text has Daniel saying, "I ate no rich food, no meat or wine entered my mouth…" (Daniel 10:3). So he did go without rich food during those three full weeks. I'd have been lost by day two, and I'm surrounded by cookie dough.

That's right, baker. Daniel was standing on the bank of the great river, the Tigris (Daniel 10:4). It was the twenty-fourth day of the first month. That's where he lifted up his eyes and saw a certain man dressed in linen.

The Jordan is a famous river, baker, so I get the pull. But Daniel says he was on the bank of the great river, the Tigris (Daniel 10:4). The Jordan isn't named anywhere in this scene. Easy one to mix up.
The Nile is a big name, baker, so it's a fair guess. But the text says Daniel was standing on the bank of the great river, the Tigris (Daniel 10:4). The Nile isn't named in this scene.

Not this time, baker. Daniel says the man's face was "…like the brilliance of lightning…" and his eyes "…like flaming torches…" (Daniel 10:6). His body was like beryl, too. That's no ordinary-looking man.

Right, baker. Daniel describes his body as "like beryl," his face "…like the brilliance of lightning…" and his eyes "…like flaming torches…" (Daniel 10:6). His voice was "…like the sound of a multitude."

Yes, baker. The men with Daniel didn't see the vision, but a great terror fell on them, and they ran and hid themselves (Daniel 10:7). Only Daniel saw the vision, and the rest took off. I'd like to say I'd stay put, but I'd be right behind them.

Calling out would be bold, baker, but that's not what these men did. The text says a great terror fell on them, and they ran and hid themselves (Daniel 10:7). Nothing there has them calling to anyone.

Yes, baker. The one speaking to Daniel says, "Stand up, for I have now been sent to you." (Daniel 10:11). He also tells Daniel to consider carefully the words he's about to say. So the reason is that he has been sent to Daniel.

The men did run off, baker, so I see where that came from. But the one speaking to Daniel says, "Stand up, for I have now been sent to you." (Daniel 10:11). Nothing there mentions the men coming back.

The three weeks were a big deal, baker, so it's easy to grab that one. But the one speaking to Daniel says, "Stand up, for I have now been sent to you." (Daniel 10:11). Nothing is said about the three weeks in that line.

Babylon is a big name, baker, so I get the guess. But the one sent to Daniel says, "…the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed me for twenty-one days." (Daniel 10:13). Persia is the name in the text. Babylon doesn't come up here.

Egypt shows up all over the Bible, baker, so I get it. But the one sent to Daniel says, "…the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed me for twenty-one days." (Daniel 10:13). No Egyptian armies in this scene.

That's the name, baker. The one sent to Daniel says, "Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me…" (Daniel 10:13). Twenty-one days of opposition, and then help shows up. I'd call that good news.

Gabriel is a well-known name, baker, and I see why it popped up. But the one sent to Daniel says, "Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me…" (Daniel 10:13). Michael is the one who comes in this verse.
Elijah is a big name, baker, so I get the guess. But he isn't named in this scene. The one sent to Daniel says, "Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me…" (Daniel 10:13).

Mourning was the mood, baker, and I get why your mind went back to it. But the one sent to Daniel says he has come to explain "…what will happen to your people in the latter days…" (Daniel 10:14). He's looking ahead, not wrapping up the mourning. Nothing in his words is about ending it.
Walking away would be a big move, baker, but that's not what Daniel does. He says, "…I set my face toward the ground and became speechless." (Daniel 10:15). Nothing there has him walking away.

Not quite, baker. Daniel says he has no strength, and then he says, "Again the one with the likeness of a man touched me and strengthened me." (Daniel 10:18). He doesn't leave Daniel to figure it out alone.

Yes, baker. Daniel says, "Again the one with the likeness of a man touched me and strengthened me." (Daniel 10:18). Daniel was not left on his own. I think that's a kind thing to see in the middle of such a scary scene.
That's the one, baker. Daniel says, "Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me." (Daniel 10:19). He had said he had no breath left, and now he's ready to listen. Quite a turnaround.
Rest sounds good, baker, and I'd have wanted it too. But Daniel says, "Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me." (Daniel 10:19). He's ready right then, with no waiting.

Yes, baker. The one speaking with Daniel says, "I must return at once to fight against the prince of Persia…" (Daniel 20:20). So he has more work waiting. He also says that when he has gone forth, the prince of Greece will come.

Those men did run off, baker, so I see how that crossed your mind. But the one speaking with Daniel says, "I must return at once to fight against the prince of Persia…" (Daniel 10:20). The men aren't part of his errand.

The mourning ran through this chapter, baker, so I get the pull. But the one speaking with Daniel says, "But first I will tell you what is inscribed in the Book of Truth." (Daniel 10:21). What comes first is the Book of Truth, not a ruling on the mourning. Nothing in his words is about how long it should last.
